section: USA elements | for tall units H. 210
source_pages: printed p.418 / PDF 420 (extracted whole: both types)
family_naming_note: Namespaced 'USA Tall H.210' for the same reason as 'Wall H.36': the registry merges section files by family NAME, and 'H.210' also names a metric tall family in the Maxima chapter (printed p.111-131) which is a different thing. The catalog's own wording is preserved in 'section'. This is the registry's first TALL-class family and its first USA elements row.
extraction_note: printed p.418 taken whole - four widths x two types, eight codes. This page was chosen as the first USA extraction over printed p.414 for one reason: p.414's four types are ALL custom-sized ('1 custom-sized fixed front', '1 custom-sized jumbo drawer'), and the Object Contract cannot yet say that a front's width comes from the opening rather than from the code. p.418 states plain fixed widths, so it extracts honestly today.
inch_note: THIS IS THE PAGE THAT PRINTS INCHES. It carries an inch column to the LEFT of the centimetre column - 18" 45.7, 24" 61, 30" 76.2, 36" 91.4 - the only place in the 634-page book that states an inch size at all. The nominal is resolved from the width by _manifest.json nominal_widths_in, which is why no nominal field appears on the rows here: a lookup, never arithmetic, and never duplicated.

data.plinth_note: OURS, NOT THE CATALOG'S. The plinth belongs to the RUN, not to this article - nothing on printed p.418 mentions one. We draw it under this panel so the plinth line does not BREAK on the drawing wherever a fridge stands in the run. Decided by Andriy 2026-08-21: draw exactly the plinth a base cabinet gets, so it is not lost on the sheet. The dishwasher door on printed p.47 deliberately gets NONE - the plinth in front of that machine really is cut away - which is why this is a per-family flag and not a rule about appliance panels.
representation_notes: WIDTH IS DRAWN NOMINAL, NEVER NET. A 30-inch panel is drawn 762 wide, although the panel actually supplied is a little narrower - and how much narrower is set by the APPLIANCE'S OWN SPECIFICATION, not by Cesar. This is the rule already in force for cabinet fronts: a 600 base unit is drawn with a 600 door and no reveal deducted. We are not producing manufacturing drawings. A run of nominal fronts reads cleanly in LayOut; a run of net fronts with reveals drawn would read as noise AND still be wrong, because the reveal is not ours to set. Confirmed by Andriy 2026-08-21.

HEIGHT NEEDS NO CUSTOMISATION, and the arithmetic is why. A standard American fridge is 84 inches = 2133,6 mm. A tall unit is 2100 standing on a 100 plinth = 2200 overall. 2200 is TALLER than the appliance, so nothing is short and nothing has to be trimmed to fit. The door extracted here serves as it stands. Worked through with Andriy 2026-08-21.

WHAT WILL NEED A CUSTOM HEIGHT is the panel that closes the 66,4 mm left over INSIDE the housing, above the appliance - not this door. That closing panel is NOT extracted, carries no code here, and must not be confused with these two types.

usa_fridge_door.notes: A PANEL, not a cabinet - it faces the client's own fridge, the same relationship the dishwasher door has to its machine on printed p.47. depth_mm is the front thickness (22, the UCON standard), not a carcass depth. THE HAND IS A DRAWING FACT HERE, NOT AN ORDER FACT, and the two must never be confused. THE ORDER CARRIES NO HAND. The description reads '1 door' and not '1 rh or lh door', which is the wording every handed unit in this catalog uses - and the difference is real, not an omission. THE TWO MARKETS INTEGRATE A FRIDGE DIFFERENTLY (explained by Andriy 2026-08-21). In Europe the appliance is built INSIDE a cabinet: the cabinet carries the hinges and its own door is linked to the appliance door by a sliding bracket, so the hand is a property of the CABINET and the factory must be told it. In America the fridge stands in a housing BETWEEN two neighbouring cabinets, or between panels, and the panel is mounted DIRECTLY on the appliance. The hand is then the appliance's business, not the cabinetry's, and the factory has no part in it. So '1 door' is the complete and correct description of the ARTICLE, and hinge_side must never be emitted for it or asked of an estimate. THE DRAWING MUST CARRY IT ANYWAY, and here is why (Andriy, 2026-08-21): fridges come hinged on one side and freezers on the other, which is sensible, but clients sometimes swap the two appliances round. The designer draws it one way, the estimate says nothing about hands because it cannot, and the problem surfaces on site when the hinges have to be moved. The elevation is the only place that information can live, so it lives there. SHOWN IN THE FRONT ELEVATION ONLY - see front_layout.hand_shown. No plan arc and no open leaf: how far and along what path this door actually swings is set by the appliance, not by us, and that projection stays PARKED until appliances are modelled. Parked 2026-08-21.

front_layout.note: One full-height panel, 2100 tall. No hinge_axis: this is not a hung door. The hand IS drawn, but in the front elevation and nowhere else - the plan arc and the open leaf both describe a swing that belongs to the appliance, and asserting one would be a drawing we cannot stand behind.

usa_wine_cooler_door.description: Door for USA fridge - 1 wine cooler door
usa_wine_cooler_door.notes: Handed in the DRAWING only, never in the order - see usa_fridge_door for the reasoning, which applies unchanged. Same four widths as the plain fridge door, one suffix apart (00 -> 01). Carries a cutout on the front, so it is not simply the other door in a different finish. The page prints two restrictions that are NOT modelled and must not be lost: (1) a surcharge of 234 points for the stainless steel protection for the wine cooler door, with NO article code - recorded here, never invented as a companion, the same treatment Servo Drive gets on the wall pages; (2) a prohibition mark against 'Maxima 2.2 with framed door' and 'Metal doors', and a positive instruction to use melamine, Technomat, Unicolor or Fenix. Finish is a composition-level axis the engine does not model at all yet (M1.6), so this restriction has nowhere to live but this note.

front_layout.note: One full-height panel, 2100 tall, with a rectangular aperture through it. The catalog dimensions neither the aperture nor its position, so the rails below are carried from appliance specifications and the hole is drawn INDICATIVE - see cutout.trust. Hand in the front elevation only, for the same reasons as the plain fridge door.

cutout.aperture_note: The aperture is DERIVED, never stored: width = panel width - 2 x rail_side, height = panel height - rail_top - rail_bottom. Every appliance maker dimensions the RAILS and lets the aperture follow, because the rails are what stay constant when the panel width changes. Storing the aperture instead would need a row per width and would disagree with itself the first time a width was added.

evidence.measured_table: _manifest.json external_specs.wine_cooler_panel_apertures - three manufacturer specifications, read 2026-08-22. The numbers live there and only there: this article takes a default from that table, it does not keep a second copy of it.
evidence.why_these_defaults: rail_side and rail_top CONVERGE across two unrelated makers (79/79/84 and 155/158/158), so 80 and 156 are defensible. rail_bottom does not converge at all (111 against 243) and 243 is taken because these are US widths meeting US appliances, while the Miele figure belongs to a 60 cm European column that never carries a 2100 front. That third number is the guess, and it is why the WHOLE aperture is marked indicative rather than only its lower edge.
evidence.cesar_side: Cesar prices this front at exactly x1.5 of the plain fridge door in every width and every finish column - 200->300, 323->484, 528->791, 665->999, 1333->2001 on CR9700/CR9701, and the same ratio on CR9400/9401, CH9700/9701, CH4640/4651. A multiplier that ignores the size of the hole is a price for the VARIANT, not for a piece of machining - the catalog's own evidence that it holds no geometry for it. Nor is there a cutout article: printed p.548 and p.554-556 list no machining line for a front. What does exist is a paid engineering service on printed p.541 (989394, 108 points, 'Feasibility study regarding cutouts and positioning'), which is the mechanism by which dimensions travel from us to the factory.
evidence.the_drawing_is_not_a_drawing: The p.418 elevation was compared vector by vector against the plain door above it (pdftocairo -svg): the SAME artwork, differing by exactly two line segments. Its frame reads 12-15 % of width at the sides and 5-6 % of height top and bottom, but the panel is drawn at 1:2.83 while the real widths run 1:2.30 to 1:3.44. Not to scale, and the left-hand view labelled 210 is a side view with no aperture at all.
evidence.open_with_elda: Whether the factory wants the aperture dimensions from us or takes them from the appliance model named in the order. One line, still unsent, in the mini-order request.
